texts.facts: The petitioner, who was the Managing Director of KINFRA- the addl.3rd respondent- is aggrieved by Ext.P10 order by which his services were terminated giving full additional charge of KINFRA to the addl. 4th respondent. The qualification prescribed were as follows: 1. The candidate should have graduation in Engineering/Equivalent or Post Graduation n Business Administration with good academic record from a recongnised University/Institution K.A.Santhosh Kumar vs The State Of Kerala on 7 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52662671/ 2 2. He/She should have at least 15 years post qualification experience of which 5 years has to be at senior levels with independent charge of a reputed organisation or a division of a large company. 3. Applicants familiar with Finance, Marketing and production functions of companies in the respective sectors will have an added advantage. 3. Petitioner submits that being a Post Graduate in Engineering from IIT, Bombay with MBA and 22 years of service in the Indian Air Force in the Engineering branch and 7 years of corporate experience in HCL Infosystems as Project Director and as Senior Vice President in the Maharashtra Border Check Post Network Ltd., he submitted application. On being successful in the interview held on 27.08.2016, he was ranked 2 in Ext.P3 select list in the sector 'Development and Infrastructure'. The additional 4th respondent was ranked 2 in the sector TRACO Cable Company Limited. Petitioner was appointed as Managing Director of KINFRA as per Ext.P4 order dated 04.10.2016. He points out that the appointment of Managing Directors were made from Ext.P3 select list, in various sectors as per Ext.P5 list. Petitioner was appointed as Managing Director of KINFRA, as per Ext.P4 order, under section 6 of Chapter III of Act 3 of 1993-the Kerala Industrial Infrastructure Development Corporation Act. It was ordered that his continuance in the post would be subject to the clearance from the Director of Vigilance and Anti Corruption Bureau and that the terms and conditions of the appointment would be fixed later. Petitioner points out that as per Ext.P6(a) letter dated 08.10.2016 he had requested the Government to fix the terms and conditions of his appointment, in order to enable him to resign from the organisation where he was working. It was stated that he was allowed to join duty only on 03.04.2017. It is stated that after his repeated requests to fix the terms and conditions of service, Government issued Ext.P8 order on 01.08.2018, according sanction to fix his pay at Rs.1.75 lakhs per month as consolidated remuneration along with perks. The petitioner submits that he joined the post under the bonafide impression and legitimate expectation that he would be able to continue at least for a period of 3 years, in the light of Ext.P7 letter dated 07.10.2006. But by Ext.P10 order the 1st respondent without any reason terminated his appointment on 25.07.2019. According to him he is made a scapegoat since he worked for the implementation of various mega projects that were of prime interest to the Government. He has pointed out 17 projects in which he was involved. He points out that his performance for 2017-18 was appreciated in Ext.P9 minutes of the meeting of the Board of KINFRA held on 31.05.2018 comparing it to the revenue generated in the previous year, referring to the execution of projects worth Rs.80.95 crores during the year 2017-18 as against Rs.45.53 crores for the year 2016-17, taking note of the improvement in the activities of KINFRA with respect to the Projects, Land Allotment, revenue generation, etc. It was also pointed out that foundation stones laid for various projects during 2017 were nearing completion and commissioning. It was stated that Mega Food Park at Palakkad, Defence Park at Ottapalam, Standard Design Factory at KINFRA Film and Video Park at Thiruvananthapuram and Kinfra Standard Design Factory at Koratty Park were some of the projects which were ready for commissioning. Apart from that he stated that about 5600 acres of land at different locations could be acquired and the proceedings for acquisition were at different stages.
texts.arguments: He pointed out that the claim towards acquisition of 77.78 acres of land at Ramanattukara, was referred for mediation; but none of the officials who were dealing with the matter informed him the fact that the Senior Government Pleader who represented the Government K.A.Santhosh Kumar vs The State Of Kerala on 7 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52662671/ 3 in the acquisition matters and the counsel who appeared for the claimants were husband and wife. It is stated that on coming to know about this he had issued memo dated 14.03.2019 directing the officials to show cause why they concealed information regarding the conflict of interest. He pointed out that the concerned official in the office of the KINFRA who concealed the aspect from him is very influential and that the order of termination is issued at that stage under his political influence. 4. The petitioner pointed out that as per Rule 3 of the Kerala Industrial Infrastructure Rules, 2008 ('the Rules' for short) Government has to fix the terms of office of the Managing Director of the Corporation and it has to be stated in the order of appointment. It is also his case that three months' notice is an implied condition for termination as in the case of resignation from the post and therefore his services were not liable to be terminated except after giving three months' notice, in accordance with Rule 8; contrary to the rules, Ext.P10 order was issued fixing his term of appointment upto 25.07.2019, the date of the order Ext.P10, simultaneously terminating his appointment, without any reason and in gross violation of the principles of natural justice. Pointing out Ext.P11 news item appeared in Times of India, regarding his termination, petitioner points out the serious damage caused to his reputation, giving way to speculations by the media that he is involved in illicit activities. According to him he was not liable to be sent out unceremoniously. 5. In the counter affidavit, respondents 1 and 2 stated that there is no specific tenure fixed for a Managing Director of KINFRA and that as per Section 6 of the Kerala Industrial Infrastructure Development Act, 1993 ('the Act' for short) which deals with the term of office of Managing Directors and conditions of services of nominated Director, the Managing Director of the Corporation shall hold office for such term as the Government may specify in this behalf. The Directors shall be entitled to draw allowances as prescribed under the Rules made under the Act. Under Rule 3 of the Kerala Industrial Infrastructure Development Rules, 2008 the Directors nominated by the Government under sub section 2 of Section 5 shall ordinarily hold office for a term of 2 years. However, the Government shall have the power to remove such Directors before the expiry of the said term, if found necessary. The term of office of the Managing Director of the Corporation shall be as fixed by the Government in the order of appointment. However, the Government may, at any time terminate the services of such Managing Director without assigning any reason. Therefore, it is stated that it was upto the Government to fix the term and even if term is fixed, to order termination even before its expiry, as per the rules as well as Ext.R1(c) order issued by the Government on 20.05.2009. Therefore, according to the respondents, the petitioner who joined as Managing Director after accepting the terms and conditions, cannot be heard to raise any contention relating to completion of any term or about any requirement of notice before termination. According to Government, Ext.P7 order issued in the year 2006 does not have any force or relevance in respect of any term of appointment. It is stated that the term of appointment of petitioner was fixed in Ext.P10 order upto 25.07.2019 and his services were terminated on that day. According to them there is no deviation from the practice in KINFRA and the manner of appointment was the same in the case of Sri.Gopala Pillai who was relieved on 07.06.2006 as per Ext.R1(f) order. It is stated that being the Managing Director the petitioner was aware of the negotiations going on with respect to the LAA cases of Ramanattukara and he himself had authorised the officials to attend the mediation. It is stated that the Vigilance Department of the Government has as per Ext.R1(i) letter dated 06.08.2019, already directed a vigilance enquiry into K.A.Santhosh Kumar vs The State Of Kerala on 7 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52662671/ 4 the loss caused to KINFRA due to lapses in conducting the case against Zoom Developers Pvt. Ltd., in respect of resumption of land leased to it. It is stated that orders of termination are effected in other PSUs also, as done in Ext.R1(j) order dated 18.02.2019. According to them, the termination is effected in accordance with Section 6 of the Act and Managing Director of a PSU has to hold office at the pleasure of Government and the Government shall have the right to remove him at any time. It is stated that the additional 4th respondent is fully qualified to be appointed as the Managing Director. 6. In the reply affidavit petitioner has produced a series of documents stating that the term of appointment of Sri.Gopala Pillai was for a period of 3 years initially on 13.4.1994; it was extended for another 3 years in 1997 and another 3 years in 2000 and thereafter in 2003 and he was relieved at his request w.e.f 04.07.2005 as per Ext.P12 series and Ext.P13. He has also produced Ext.P15 order relating to the appointment of another M.D in the year 2011 and his extension in 2014 pointing out that the tenure of those appointments were for 3 years and that there is no reason for adopting a different yardstick in his case. According to him after illegally terminating his appointment, the respondents have given full additional charge to additional 4th respondent who does not have any qualification for the same, that too after the select list was cancelled. According to the petitioner if at all he was to be replaced appointment ought to have been made as ordered in Ext.P18. 7. In the additional counter affidavit, respondents 1 and 2 stated that the term fixed in the case of others in 1994, 1997, etc as the Managing Director cannot be treated as a precedent, because of the advancement in the sector of industrial and infrastructure in tune with the global developments in various aspects like economy, population, etc. It is further stated that the additional 4 th respondent who was appointed in his place is having all the requisite qualifications and he had submitted Ext.R1(i) application for the sectors Development&Infrastructural Agencies, Engineering and Electrical Equipment and Electronics. At the same time it is stated that in Ext.R1(k) application submitted by the petitioner his preference was only for the sectors of Engineering, and Electrical Equipment and Electronics. Relying on Ext.R1(m) attendance sheet for the interview held on 07.09.2016, it is stated that the petitioner had not applied for the industrial sector whereas Mr.Santhosh Koshy Thomas had applied for it. According to the respondents a selection process as per Ext.P18 G.O on 26.05.2018 was not necessary when qualified hands were available for appointments. It is further stated that there is a practice of appointing Managing Director of one PSU as the Managing Director of another PSU as the selection was on the basis of a single process and the additional 4th respondent was found eligible and competent to be the Managing Director of PSU. According to them petitioner deviated from his duty as Managing Director in dealing with the case pending before the Madhyapradesh High Court in respect of resumption of land from M/s.Zoom Developers and he failed to safeguard the interest of KINFRA. 8. Additional respondent nos.3 and 4 have filed separate counter affidavits stating that petitioner did not even submit application for appointment in the sector Development&Infrastructure whereas the 4th respondent had applied for the same. According to them it is not necessary to assign reasons or issue notice before termination of the appointment of petitioner. According to them the works which the petitioner claimed to have completed or were nearing completion, were already completed K.A.Santhosh Kumar vs The State Of Kerala on 7 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52662671/ 5 even before he took charge. It is stated that the litigation before the MadhyaPradesh High Court against M/s.Zoom Developers started during the tenure of petitioner and it resulted in adverse orders against KINFRA since petitioner did not take any steps to safeguard its interest. 9. The additional respondent No.4 in his counter affidavit, explaining his qualifications, stated that he is fully qualified to be appointed as the Managing Director of KINFRA. He was given additional charge of the KINFRA while terminating the appointment of the petitioner and that appointment was to a sector for which he had submitted application whereas there was no application from the petitioner for appointment in that sector. He was initially appointed as the Managing Director of TRACO Cables Company under the Electrical Equipment category. It is stated that he worked in senior management level as Director, Executive Director etc. during the last 20 years before his appointment as Managing Director. 10. The petitioner filed reply affidavits to the counter affidavits of all the respondents. He stated that even if no reason is to be assigned while terminating the services, reasons should be available in the files leading to the termination. He stated that the notes furnished along with Ext.P20 letter dated 17.09.2019 of the State Public Information Officer do not reveal any reason for termination of his service; on the other hand it would appear that there was no reason at all as evident from the noting of the Principal Secretary that due process for removal was not followed as per the principles of natural justice. According to the petitioner he was relieved at the instance of the Private Secretary to the Minister of Industries Department. It was also pointed out that the information relating to the appearance of the concerned Government Pleader in the land acquisition cases who represented the state when his wife was the Counsel appearing for the claimants, was not brought to his notice by the official of KINFRA who was dealing with the matter; it is stated that he had already issued memos to that official for not furnishing the relevant information. He also stated that the lease of land to M/s.Zoom Developers and its resumption in 2016 took place prior to his joining as the Managing Director. It was also stated that he acted on the advice of the standing counsel of KINFRA. Petitioner also produced Exts.P21 to P24 pointing out that his appointment as the Managing Director in KINFRA was on the basis of his performance in the interview whereas the application of the 4th respondent in the Development&Infrastructure sector was rejected and no other person was selected for KINFRA. He also pointed out that Government have appointed Managing Directors in various Public Sector Undertakings from the select list prepared by the Public Enterprises Selection Board and the method of selection has been modified in 2019 and therefore the 4 th respondent is not a person who is selected in accordance with rules for appointment as the Managing Director of KINFRA. The main contention of the petitioner is that he was entitled to continue as the Managing Director for a period of three years, in the light of Ext.P7 order and that termination of his appointment before he completed his tenure is unsustainable. But a perusal of the order of his appointment would show that no tenure is provided in it. Under Section 6 of the KINFRA Act K.A.Santhosh Kumar vs The State Of Kerala on 7 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52662671/ 6 (Ext.R1(a))the Managing Director of the Corporation shall be appointed by the Government and he shall hold office for such term as the Government may specify. Even though the petitioner had requested to fix the terms and conditions of his appointment as per Ext.P6 and Ext.P6(a) letters on 07.10.2016 and 08.10.2016, it was only as per Ext.P8 order that the Government responded to that, that too according sanction only for fixing his monthly remuneration at Rs.1.75 lakhs. Clause 3 thereof provides that "appointment as MD/CEO of a Company/PSU shall be at the pleasure of the Government. Government shall have the right to remove him from the post at any time (although the order of appointment will indicate a fixed term for such appointment). When no term is fixed for the appointment, the question of reason in support of termination does K.A.Santhosh Kumar vs The State Of Kerala on 7 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52662671/ 7 not arise. 15. The learned counsel for the petitioner relied on the judgment of the Division Bench in Ashok v. Chancellor, Kerala Veterinary and Animal Sciences University : 2012 (3) KLT 829 and the judgment of the Apex Court in Union of India and others vs. Major S.P.Sharma and others : (2014) 6 SCC 351 in support of his contention that the termination was illegal, in the absence of availability of any reasons at least in the files, even when the petitioner held his appointment at the pleasure of Government. In the judgment in Ashok's case the Division Bench was considering the validity of the termination of services of the Vice Chancellor of Kerala Veterinary and Animal Sciences University, before the expiry of 5 years of his appointment, in contravention of section 12(7) of the KVASU Act, according to which the Vice Chancellor shall hold the office for a period of 5 years subject to the pleasure of the Chancellor and the provisions of sub section 6. Referring to the judgments of the apex court with respect to the doctrine of pleasure in B.P. Singhal v. Union of India: 2010 (6) SCC 331, this court held that the doctrine of pleasure does not mean a licence to act arbitrarily, capriciously or whimsically. It was held therein that the discretionary powers conferred on public authority would be exercised reasonably and for public good. It was found that the revocation of appointment of the Vice Chancellor was not for any administrative reason as it was found that the action was initiated on the basis of an article he had written and published in the Indian Express Newspaper. But in the present case no term was fixed and it cannot be said that there was a premature termination. 16. In the judgment in Union of India v. S.P.Sharma [(2014) 6 SCC 351], the Apex Court was considering a case where the termination of services of 2 Army personnel after court martial proceedings were defended in the light of Section 18 of the Army Act read with Article 310 of the Constitution, namely, exercise of doctrine of pleasure. The Army Personnel alleged violation of Article 311 (2) of the Constitution of India. It was held that while exercising judicial review the court cannot substitute its own conclusions on the basis of materials on record, especially in a case where the safety and security of the nation was involved and the tenure of services of such army personnel are at the pleasure of the President and officers can be removed by the authority on whose pleasure he holds office without assigning any reason. However it approved the constitution Bench judgment in B.P Singhal v. Union of India [(2010) 6 SCC 331]. In B.P. Singhal's case he apex court while considering the question of removal of Governors held that the doctrine of pleasure does not mean a licence to act arbitrarily, capriciously or whimsically and that it is presumed that discretionary powers conferred on any public authority will necessarily be exercised reasonably and for the public good. It was held that though no notice need be issued or reasons be assigned, there should be some valid cause for withdrawal of the pleasure and that it cannot be at the sweet will, whim and fancy of the authority. It was also held that the controlling factor in determining whether the exercise of prerogative power is subject to judicial review is not its source but its subject-matter. It was also held that the extent or scope of judicial review for one will be different from the scope of judicial review for the other. It is pertinent to note that the order of appointment of petitioner did not K.A.Santhosh Kumar vs The State Of Kerala on 7 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52662671/ 8 contain any assurance to retain him for any particular period. 17. In the judgment in Retd. Armed Forces Medical Association & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors: (2006) 11 SCC 731, relied on by the learned Government Pleader, the Apex Court was considering the validity of appointment of the Chief Engineer of the establishment as its Managing Director without fixing any tenure. The Apex Court held that when the Act and the Rules have not prescribed any definite term or any particular mode, the appointing authority has absolute discretion in the matter. It was a case where a writ of quo-warranto was sought against the appellant therein. The contention was that Section 6(1) of the Karnataka Urban Water Supply and Drainage Board Act 1973 which provided that the Managing Director shall hold office during the pleasure of the Government would not mean to have conferred any arbitrary or unfettered right to Government to retain him, misusing its discretionary power to extend his tenure. In para.44 of the said judgment the Apex Court found as follows: "44. In the instant case, the power to appoint the Managing Director of the Board is vested in the Board under Section 4(2) of the Act. Neither the Act nor the Rules prescribed any mode of appointment or tenure of appointment. When the mode of appointment, tenure of appointment have been left to the discretion of the Government by the Act and the Rules, and the Act makes it clear that the Managing Director shall hold office at the pleasure of the Government, the High Court could not have fettered the discretion of the Government by holding that Section 4(2) of the Act does not expressly give the power to the State Government to make ad hoc or contractual appointment. It is well settled that when the statute does not lay down the method of appointment or term of appointment and when the Act specifies that the appointment is one of sure tenure, the appointing authority who has the power to appoint has absolute discretion in the matter and it cannot be said that discretion to appoint does not include the power to appoint on contract basis. 18. It is relevant to note the judgment in WP(C) No.29558/2017, relied on by the learned Government Pleader where the petitioner sought re-appointment as a Managing Director stating K.A.Santhosh Kumar vs The State Of Kerala on 7 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52662671/ 9 that he was only relieved from the post and there was no termination.

It was also pointed out that the information relating to the appearance of the concerned Government Pleader in the land acquisition cases who represented the state when his wife was the Counsel appearing for the claimants, was not brought to his notice by the official of KINFRA who was dealing with the matter; it is stated that he had already issued memos to that official for not furnishing the relevant information. He also stated that the lease of land to M/s.Zoom Developers and its resumption in 2016 took place prior to his joining as the Managing Director. It was also stated that he acted on the advice of the standing counsel of KINFRA. Petitioner also produced Exts.P21 to P24 pointing out that his appointment as the Managing Director in KINFRA was on the basis of his performance in the interview whereas the application of the 4th respondent in the Development&Infrastructure sector was rejected and no other person was selected for KINFRA. He also pointed out that Government have appointed Managing Directors in various Public Sector Undertakings from the select list prepared by the Public Enterprises Selection Board and the method of selection has been modified in 2019 and therefore the 4 th respondent is not a person who is selected in accordance with rules for appointment as the Managing Director of KINFRA. But a perusal of the order of his appointment would show that no tenure is provided in it. When no term is fixed for the appointment, the question of reason in support of termination does K.A.Santhosh Kumar vs The State Of Kerala on 7 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52662671/ 7 not arise. 15. The learned counsel for the petitioner relied on the judgment of the Division Bench in Ashok v. Chancellor, Kerala Veterinary and Animal Sciences University : 2012 (3) KLT 829 and the judgment of the Apex Court in Union of India and others vs. Major S.P.Sharma and others : (2014) 6 SCC 351 in support of his contention that the termination was illegal, in the absence of availability of any reasons at least in the files, even when the petitioner held his appointment at the pleasure of Government. 18. It is relevant to note the judgment in WP(C) No.29558/2017, relied on by the learned Government Pleader where the petitioner sought re-appointment as a Managing Director stating K.A.Santhosh Kumar vs The State Of Kerala on 7 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52662671/ 9 that he was only relieved from the post and there was no termination.
texts.respondent_arguments: The main contention of the petitioner is that he was entitled to continue as the Managing Director for a period of three years, in the light of Ext.P7 order and that termination of his appointment before he completed his tenure is unsustainable. Even though the petitioner had requested to fix the terms and conditions of his appointment as per Ext.P6 and Ext.P6(a) letters on 07.10.2016 and 08.10.2016, it was only as per Ext.P8 order that the Government responded to that, that too according sanction only for fixing his monthly remuneration at Rs.1.75 lakhs.
texts.other_lawyer_arguments: Under Section 6 of the KINFRA Act K.A.Santhosh Kumar vs The State Of Kerala on 7 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52662671/ 6 (Ext.R1(a))the Managing Director of the Corporation shall be appointed by the Government and he shall hold office for such term as the Government may specify. Clause 3 thereof provides that "appointment as MD/CEO of a Company/PSU shall be at the pleasure of the Government. Government shall have the right to remove him from the post at any time (although the order of appointment will indicate a fixed term for such appointment). In the judgment in Ashok's case the Division Bench was considering the validity of the termination of services of the Vice Chancellor of Kerala Veterinary and Animal Sciences University, before the expiry of 5 years of his appointment, in contravention of section 12(7) of the KVASU Act, according to which the Vice Chancellor shall hold the office for a period of 5 years subject to the pleasure of the Chancellor and the provisions of sub section 6. Referring to the judgments of the apex court with respect to the doctrine of pleasure in B.P. Singhal v. Union of India: 2010 (6) SCC 331, this court held that the doctrine of pleasure does not mean a licence to act arbitrarily, capriciously or whimsically. It was held therein that the discretionary powers conferred on public authority would be exercised reasonably and for public good. It was found that the revocation of appointment of the Vice Chancellor was not for any administrative reason as it was found that the action was initiated on the basis of an article he had written and published in the Indian Express Newspaper. But in the present case no term was fixed and it cannot be said that there was a premature termination. 16. In the judgment in Union of India v. S.P.Sharma [(2014) 6 SCC 351], the Apex Court was considering a case where the termination of services of 2 Army personnel after court martial proceedings were defended in the light of Section 18 of the Army Act read with Article 310 of the Constitution, namely, exercise of doctrine of pleasure. The Army Personnel alleged violation of Article 311 (2) of the Constitution of India. It was held that while exercising judicial review the court cannot substitute its own conclusions on the basis of materials on record, especially in a case where the safety and security of the nation was involved and the tenure of services of such army personnel are at the pleasure of the President and officers can be removed by the authority on whose pleasure he holds office without assigning any reason. However it approved the constitution Bench judgment in B.P Singhal v. Union of India [(2010) 6 SCC 331]. In B.P. Singhal's case he apex court while considering the question of removal of Governors held that the doctrine of pleasure does not mean a licence to act arbitrarily, capriciously or whimsically and that it is presumed that discretionary powers conferred on any public authority will necessarily be exercised reasonably and for the public good. It was held that though no notice need be issued or reasons be assigned, there should be some valid cause for withdrawal of the pleasure and that it cannot be at the sweet will, whim and fancy of the authority. It was also held that the controlling factor in determining whether the exercise of prerogative power is subject to judicial review is not its source but its subject-matter. It was also held that the extent or scope of judicial review for one will be different from the scope of judicial review for the other. It is pertinent to note that the order of appointment of petitioner did not K.A.Santhosh Kumar vs The State Of Kerala on 7 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/52662671/ 8 contain any assurance to retain him for any particular period. 17. In the judgment in Retd. Armed Forces Medical Association & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors: (2006) 11 SCC 731, relied on by the learned Government Pleader, the Apex Court was considering the validity of appointment of the Chief Engineer of the establishment as its Managing Director without fixing any tenure. The Apex Court held that when the Act and the Rules have not prescribed any definite term or any particular mode, the appointing authority has absolute discretion in the matter. It was a case where a writ of quo-warranto was sought against the appellant therein. The contention was that Section 6(1) of the Karnataka Urban Water Supply and Drainage Board Act 1973 which provided that the Managing Director shall hold office during the pleasure of the Government would not mean to have conferred any arbitrary or unfettered right to Government to retain him, misusing its discretionary power to extend his tenure. In para.44 of the said judgment the Apex Court found as follows: "44. In the instant case, the power to appoint the Managing Director of the Board is vested in the Board under Section 4(2) of the Act. Neither the Act nor the Rules prescribed any mode of appointment or tenure of appointment. When the mode of appointment, tenure of appointment have been left to the discretion of the Government by the Act and the Rules, and the Act makes it clear that the Managing Director shall hold office at the pleasure of the Government, the High Court could not have fettered the discretion of the Government by holding that Section 4(2) of the Act does not expressly give the power to the State Government to make ad hoc or contractual appointment. It is well settled that when the statute does not lay down the method of appointment or term of appointment and when the Act specifies that the appointment is one of sure tenure, the appointing authority who has the power to appoint has absolute discretion in the matter and it cannot be said that discretion to appoint does not include the power to appoint on contract basis.
